newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban conquest changes map of Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Taleban conquest changes map of Afghanistan.

text.p: The capture by the Islamic Taleban of the opposition stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif on Saturday has fundamentally changed the map of Afghanistan and put in doubt the opposition's ability to survive in its truncated form.
Before Saturday's loss, the opposition controlled 25 percent of the country. Mazar-i-Sharif was their capital and logistical centre.
When they lost Mazar, they lost the fertile plains that surround it and the roads that were vital for the resupply of other opposition fronts.
After Saturday's losses, the opposition controls less than 10 percent of the country and is stranded in Afghanistan's mountainous northeast and central provinces.

They are now concentrated in two main areas: the Bamiyan valley, which is populated mainly by Shi'ite Moslems loyal to the Hezb-e-Wahadat party; and Badakhshan and the Panjsher valley, which is politically dominated by loyalists of Jamiat-e-Islami, the party of the government the Taleban ousted from Kabul in September last year.
Bamiyan is starting to look vulnerable, according to one analyst of the events in Afghanistan.
The opposition appeared to suffer a further loss on Sunday when a Pakistan-based Afghan news service reported that the far northern province of Kunduz which it held had fallen to the Taleban.

"Hezb-e-Wahadat are almost totally surrounded by the Taleban. Most of their supplies came through Mazar, and those that didn't are also vulnerable to the Taleban now they have taken Mazar," said the analyst, who asked not to be identified.
"They have put up a fierce fight against the Taleban, but isolated as they are now, they are in trouble," he said.

Jamiat-e-Islami, led by ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani and his chief military commander Ahmed Shah Masood, fled to the Panjsher valley and Badakhshan in the wake of their defeat in Kabul by the Taleban in September.
Masood achieved fame as a commander fighting the Soviet forces from bases in the Panjsher in the 1980s.

They still have a land link to the relatively friendly borders of Tajikistan, albeit over terrain that is impassable to vehicles. They are reputed to have a large stock of weapons and ammunition in the Panjsher valley.

"Masood is one of the most able commanders in Afghanistan, but I am not sure how much longer his people will be willing to fight against the Taleban, who are both Afghans and, on past form, unbeatable," said the analyst.
"History has shown that in Afghanistan's wars, morale is as important as weapons, and that is going to be difficult to maintain in the wake of the loss of Mazar," he said.
It was not possible to contact the opposition on Sunday morning.
The opposition received political backing from Russia, and the central Asian states of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, who were worried about the spread of radical Islam on their southern borders.

But with the loss of the opposition's most significant territory, and the seeming inevitability of the Taleban's role as the future rulers of Afghanistan, economic considerations will weigh heavily with the opposition's former backers.

Afghanistan holds the key to trade between the energy-rich states of central Asia and the Indian sub-continent. Good relations with Afghanistan's new rulers will be vital to fully exploit the potential of their resources.
